sections.title: Board connections and controls
sourceHeadings: The Board: This Lesson's Pins
sections.body:
A **board label** identifies a physical connection. **ADC** converts joystick/knob voltage to numbers; **USART** sends serial data through **TX** (transmit) and **RX** (receive). **I²C** uses **SDA** (data) and **SCL** (clock). **OLED** means organic light-emitting diode display; **GND** is ground and **3V3** is a 3.3 V supply.

Nucleo-C031C6/MB1717 exposes outer ST morpho double rows and inner Arduino A0–A5/D0–D15 rows. Some signals share labels, for example PA5/D13.

Use the actual connected header position. Power is 3V3 and GND.

PA0/PA1 are joystick ADC IN0/IN1. PA4 is ADC IN4 for the knob.

PA2/PA3 USART2 TX/RX. PA6 TIM3_CH1 buzzer.

PB8/PB9 I²C1 SCL/SDA for OLED at 0x3C. PB4/PB5 buttons A/B and PB3 stick select.

A arms. B injects a gust.

SEL selects SIM/MPU. Knob adjusts rate Kp.

MPU6050 at 0x68 shares the OLED bus.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads pin levels; **MODER** chooses mode; **AFR** chooses alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug, the programming/debug connection.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal. Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly.

sections.title: How Do We Fly a Drone Without a Drone?
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: How Do We Fly a Drone Without a Drone?
sections.body:
**Software-in-the-loop (SITL)** runs the controller against a software aircraft. The world task computes motion; control chooses motor commands. An **ESC** is a motor’s electronic speed controller.

A 500 Hz world task supplies samples to 250 Hz control.

The PC runner links the same world.c and control.c. A real MPU 6050 and ESC driver could replace the world behind the same interface.

The proposed Webots environment was unavailable, so physics moved into firmware. Include its CPU use in the budget.

The host can grade a 30 s simulated flight rapidly. This plant has four motors.

sections.title: Frames and Signs
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: Frames and Signs
sections.body:
**Body axes** move with the aircraft. **Roll** tilts the sides; **pitch** raises/lowers the nose; **yaw** turns it left/right. **CW/CCW** mean clockwise/counterclockwise.

Use forward/right/down body axes. Positive roll lowers the right side, positive pitch raises the nose and positive yaw turns the nose right.

Looking down: M0 front-left CW, M1 front-right CCW, M2 rear-right CW, M3 rear-left CCW. Increasing left thrust rolls right.

Increasing front thrust pitches up. Increasing CCW thrust yaws right.

A stationary level accelerometer reports (0,0,−9.81), because specific force points upward.

sections.title: The Plant — a Quadcopter on a Gimbal
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: The Plant — a Quadcopter on a Gimbal
sections.body:
The **plant** is the controlled system or its simulation. A **gimbal** fixes its centre. **Torque** turns it; **inertia** resists rotation changes. A **quaternion** stores orientation without Euler-angle singularities.

The model has no translation. Four lagged motors produce X-layout torques; Euler rigid-body dynamics and quaternion integration update rotation.

The cross-product term couples axes; damping removes energy like friction. The model keeps its crashed state after tilt exceeds 90°.

| Parameter | Value | Why that number |
|---|---|---|
| mass, arm | 0.5 kg, 0.12 m | a 250-class quad |
| inertia *Ixx, Iyy, Izz* | 0.004, 0.004, 0.007 kg·m² | yaw is hardest to turn |
| thrust per motor | 0–4 N, linear in command | thrust/weight 3.3 |
| motor lag | first order, τ = 30 ms | props have inertia |
| drag torque | 0.016 m × thrust | the only thing that yaws a quad |
| rate | 500 Hz (`WORLD_DT` = 2 ms) | twice the controller |

```text
I w' = tau - w x (I w) - c w
```

sections.title: Four Thrusts, Three Torques
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: Four Thrusts, Three Torques
sections.body:
**Thrust** is a motor’s lifting force. Differences between four thrusts produce roll, pitch and yaw torque. **Motor lag** delays the force response.

The torque equations below map motor thrusts T 0…T 3 into body roll, pitch and yaw. With d=0.12/√2≈0.085 m and 4 N full-scale motor thrust, a ±u roll pattern produces 339 u rad/s².

At u=0.1 this is about 34 rad/s² or 1900°/s². Commands remain bounded at 0 and 1 and the response has a 30 ms motor lag, so ideal torque authority does not imply instantaneous correction.

```c
float tx = d * (T[0] + T[3] - T[1] - T[2]);
float ty = d * (T[0] + T[1] - T[2] - T[3]);
float tz = w->k_drag * (T[1] + T[3] - T[0] - T[2]);
```

```text
d * 4 * (u * 4 N) / Ixx = 0.085 * 16 / 0.004 * u  =  339 u   rad/s^2
```

sections.title: The Simulated IMU — Built to Be Annoying
sourceHeadings: Slide 6: The Simulated IMU — Built to Be Annoying
sections.body:
**Bias** is a persistent offset; **random walk** makes an offset wander. **Noise** varies between readings. A **low-pass filter** smooths fast changes but delays them.

The table specifies sensor errors, motor vibration and the 44 Hz filter.

Seeded xorshift noise makes tests repeatable. The gravity direction expressed in the body's axes comes from the rotation matrix and specific force has the opposite sign.

Holding the centre of mass fixed makes accelerometer tilt usable: in free flight the sensor also sees thrust and translational acceleration, so it need not indicate gravity during manoeuvres.

| Imperfection | In `world.c` | What it does to you |
|---|---|---|
| gyro **bias** | +0.8, −0.6, +0.4 °/s, plus a slow random walk | integrated, it drifts without limit |
| gyro noise | 0.3 °/s, 1σ | small |
| accel noise | 0.3 m/s² (0.03 g), 1σ | small |
| **motor vibration** | 6 m/s² × mean motor: ~0.19 g at hover | tilt from accel jumps by degrees |
| **low-pass filter** | first order, 44 Hz (the chip's `DLPF_CFG = 3`) | smooth — and ~4 ms **late** |

sections.title: Tilt From Gravity — Right on Average, Noisy Every Sample
sourceHeadings: Slide 7: Tilt From Gravity — Right on Average, Noisy Every Sample
sections.body:
Vibration can look like tilt without actual turning. **atan2** finds an angle from two components; **sqrt** takes a square root.

Gravity-based tilt uses atan 2(−ay,−az) for roll and atan 2(ax,√(ay²+az²)) for pitch. The lightweight fmath approximations avoid about 4 KB of libm.

Gravity gives a bounded long-term reference, but vibration of 0.19 g can mimic an 11° instantaneous tilt. Host accelerometer-only results are 3.2° RMS error, 7.2° peak and 6.0° changes between adjacent 4 ms samples.

```c
s.roll_acc  = f_atan2(-ay, -az);
s.pitch_acc = f_atan2(ax, f_sqrt(ay * ay + az * az));
```

sections.title: Tilt From the Gyro — Smooth, and Wrong by Tomorrow
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Tilt From the Gyro — Smooth, and Wrong by Tomorrow
sections.body:
A **gyro** measures turning speed. **Integration** adds rate×elapsed time, so constant rate bias accumulates into angle error.

Integrating gyro rate gives smooth small-angle attitude, but also integrates bias. A 0.8°/s bias accumulates 48° per minute.

Host gyro-only flight after 30 s has 14.5° RMS estimation error and a 26° worst error. The real plant leans while the controller believes it is level.

An estimate-based tilt failsafe cannot detect a failure hidden by that same estimate.

```text
roll(t + dt) = roll(t) + p * dt          (small angles: roll' = p)
```

sections.title: What a Gyro Bias Costs, Predicted
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: What a Gyro Bias Costs, Predicted
sections.body:
At **equilibrium**, gyro bias injection balances gravity correction, leaving a bounded angle offset.

Remaining angle error is bias×τ: 0.8×0.196≈0.16°.

Increasing α smooths vibration but retains more bias. Reducing it improves bias rejection but passes noise.

The host RMS of 0.20° at α=0.98 includes noise in addition to the predicted bias offset.

```text
error = bias × τ  =  0.8 °/s × 0.196 s  =  0.16°
```

sections.title: Alpha, Measured
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Alpha, Measured
sections.body:
**Jitter** is change between neighbouring samples. **RMS** (root mean square) summarizes typical error magnitude. Smoothness alone does not establish accuracy.

This table is a host measurement over a 30 s hover with gyro biases +0.8/−0.6°/s and vibration. Error means estimate minus true roll.

Jitter compares adjacent 4 ms estimates; true tilt is actual attitude.

Jitter declines as α rises, but total estimation error has a minimum near 0.98. At 0.995, roughly 0.64° predicted bias exceeds the noise benefit.

These are model/host results, not observed OLED or Wokwi performance.

| alpha | τ | error RMS | error max | jitter RMS | true tilt max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (accel only) | 0 | 3.18° | 7.18° | 5.97° | 0.7° |
| 0.90 | 36 ms | 0.33° | 1.32° | 0.33° | 0.7° |
| **0.98** (default) | 196 ms | **0.20°** | **0.57°** | 0.064° | 0.5° |
| 0.995 | 0.8 s | 0.60° | 0.79° | 0.016° | 0.8° |
| 1 (gyro only) | ∞ | 14.54° | 26.15° | 0.002° | **26.2°** |

sections.title: Two Loops, One Inside the Other
sourceHeadings: Slide 12: Two Loops, One Inside the Other
sections.body:
A **control loop** repeatedly measures and corrects error. A **cascade** nests loops; **bandwidth** describes their response speed.

The outer proportional angle loop requests angular rate: gain 9 turns 10° angle error into 90°/s, clamped at ±200°/s. The inner rate PID uses the gyro directly and converts rate error into differences in motor thrust every 4 ms.

The fast rate servo damps inertia before the slower angle loop steers it. A cascade requires a substantial inner-to-outer bandwidth separation.

sections.title: The Rate PID, Line by Line
sourceHeadings: Slide 13: The Rate PID, Line by Line
sections.body:
**Proportional (P)** reacts to current error; **integral (I)** accumulates it; **derivative (D)** reacts to change. Here D uses measured rate.

The table gives gains. Negative measured-rate differentiation supplies damping.

A 0.5 update factor low-passes that derivative. The integral is already in output units.

Limit output to ±0.25. Measurement-based D avoids a setpoint-change impulse.

| Term | Gain | Job |
|---|---|---|
| P | 0.12 × knob | 1 rad/s off → 12 % differential thrust |
| I | 0.15 | trims out what P cannot: a motor slightly weaker than the rest |
| D | 0.0008, on the **measurement**, low-passed | damping without a "derivative kick" when the setpoint steps |
| clamp | ±0.25 | no axis may take more than a quarter of the motor range |

```c
float d = -(meas - *meas_prev) * CTRL_HZ;
*meas_prev = meas;
*dfilt += 0.5f * (d - *dfilt);
float u_free = k * t->rate_kp * e + t->rate_kd * *dfilt + *integ;
float u = f_clamp(u_free, -t->max_out, t->max_out);
```

sections.title: Saturation — Asking for More Than Exists
sourceHeadings: Slide 16: Saturation — Asking for More Than Exists
sections.body:
Legal axis corrections can still combine into an excessive motor command. **Saturation** is the physical limit reached by a request.

Apply the three table limits. Motor clipping sets saturated for the next anti-windup step.

At throttle 0.35, downward command room is only 0.35, so upper and lower authority differ. A 60° stick error would otherwise request 540°/s.

| Clamp | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| rate setpoint ±200 °/s | angle loop | a 60° stick error must not ask for 540 °/s |
| axis output ±0.25 | rate loop | roll must not starve pitch of motor range |
| motor 0..1 | after the mixer | physics; and it raises `saturated` |

sections.title: When Not to Fly
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: When Not to Fly
sections.body:
**Arming** permits motors to operate. A **failsafe** removes permission after a fault. A **latched trip** requires deliberate operator reset.

Safety checks run every 4 ms. Arming needs throttle below 0.05, 125 good samples (0.5 s) and tilt below 25°.

Flight trips past 60°, on unhealthy/non-finite/out-of-range IMU values (>2000°/s or >16 g), or five unchanged sequence steps (20 ms). A trip latches until the arm switch is cycled.

| Rule | Threshold | Why |
|---|---|---|
| arm only with **throttle low** | < 0.05 | a drone that arms at half throttle leaps at your face |
| arm only after **0.5 s of good samples** | `CTRL_SETTLE_STEPS` 125 | right after reset the estimate has not caught up |
| arm only when **level** | < 25° | not upside down in the grass |
| **disarm** past 60° tilt | `CTRL_TILT_LIMIT` | it is crashing; stop the props |
| **disarm** on a non-finite or absurd reading | NaN, > 2000 °/s, > 16 g | a broken IMU must not fly |
| **disarm** if `seq` freezes | 5 steps = 20 ms | a dead driver returns the last value forever |
| re-arm only after the switch is **cycled** | | a failsafe must not re-arm itself |

Settling was added after a host test armed at 30°: new filters initially reported level.

Use !(abs(x)<35) to reject NaN: NaN makes ordinary greater-than comparisons false, so x>35 alone fails open.

sections.title: Too Little, Too Much — the Knob
sourceHeadings: Slide 19: Too Little, Too Much — the Knob
sections.body:
**Gain** scales correction. Too little inner-loop gain permits large swings; too much exposes sensor and motor delays.

The logarithmic knob spans ×0.125 to ×8. Each eighth-turn doubles P scale.

The host table measures a 20° roll step. Very low gain makes the inner loop too slow for the angle loop: ×0.125 reaches 59° and never settles.

Very high gain exposes phase lag from the sensor, 4 ms sampling and 30 ms motors: ×8 has 19.2°/s remaining rate RMS. Default ×1 settles in 0.34 s with 0.3% overshoot.

The sensor low-pass corner is 44 Hz.

| Kp scale | rise | overshoot | settle (±1°) | rate RMS after 2 s | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ×0.125 | 0.16 s | **194 %** | never | **235 °/s** | swings to 59°, 1° short of the failsafe |
| ×0.25 | 0.13 s | 44.5 % | 2.17 s | 7.2 °/s | sloppy |
| ×0.5 | 0.12 s | 13.5 % | 0.57 s | 1.0 °/s | |
| **×1** | 0.20 s | 0.3 % | **0.34 s** | 1.1 °/s | default |
| ×2 | 0.20 s | 0.4 % | 0.35 s | 1.0 °/s | |

sections.title: Five Tasks on One Core
sourceHeadings: Slide 20: Five Tasks on One Core
sections.body:
A **task** is scheduled work. **Priority** selects the next ready task. A **snapshot** copies related fields from one consistent instant.

The task table places physical simulation above control, pilot processing, shell and display. Pilot work also ramps throttle, sends 25 Hz attitude telemetry and manages beeps.

A 52-byte sensors_t requires a coherent copy: brief interrupt masking prevents gyro and acceleration fields from different world steps being mixed. Display rate must not determine the control period.

| Task | Rate | Priority | Does |
|---|---|---|---|
| world | 500 Hz | 5 (most urgent) | `world_step` + `world_sense` → `g_sens` |
| ctrl | 250 Hz | 4 | `g_sens` → `control_step` → `g_act` |
| pilot | 50 Hz | 3 | joystick, buttons, knob, throttle ramp, `$ATT` at 25 Hz, beeps |
| shell | on input | 2 | `stats`, `alpha`, `aw`, `mix`, `kick`, `hold` |
| disp | 15 Hz | 1 | horizon, motor bars, flush to the OLED |

```c
__disable_irq(); in = g_sens; __enable_irq();
```

sections.title: Counting Cycles With SysTick
sourceHeadings: Slide 21: Counting Cycles With SysTick
sections.body:
**SysTick** is the kernel’s hardware down-counter. A **wrap** reloads it at zero. **Interrupt masking** temporarily prevents handlers from running.

SysTick is kernel-owned at 1 kHz and 48 MHz: LOAD=47999, VAL counts down, and both meaningful fields are bits 23:0 at SysTick base 0xE000E010. The elapsed-cycle function below allows one wrap.

Measurements mask interrupts, so they must be shorter than one tick and occur only once per 64 steps. Frequent roughly 0.7 ms blackouts could lose UART bytes. stats exposes target readings.

| Register / function | Width, value and bit fields |
|---|---|
| LOAD  —  SYST_RVR, 47999 here | 32; 23:0 RELOAD |
| VAL  —  SYST_CVR, counts down | 32; 23:0 CURRENT |

```c
static inline uint32_t cyc_elapsed(uint32_t v0, uint32_t v1)
{
    return v0 >= v1 ? v0 - v1 : v0 + (SysTick->LOAD + 1u) - v1;
}
```

sections.title: The Budget — the Plant Costs More Than the Pilot
sourceHeadings: Slide 22: The Budget — the Plant Costs More Than the Pilot
sections.body:
A **flash wait state** adds instruction-fetch delay. An **instruction model** estimates execution cost; the board runs both physics and control.

The table uses lesson 10's instruction timing model on the actual Main.elf at one flash wait state, not a Wokwi observation. Moving repeated divisions outside the loop, generating noise with integers and using a 64-entry sine table reduce world/control load from 72.8% to 48.8%.

The unchanged flight controller costs about 25938 cycles, or 540 µs per 4 ms. Zero wait states predict 34.1%.

Simulation sensor synthesis originally exceeded controller cost. Real external physics does not consume MCU cycles.

| Version | `world_step` | `world_sense` | `control_step` flying | world + control CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first draft | 18 789 | 38 097 | 25 926 | **72.8 %** |
| divides hoisted; noise from integers | 17 405 | 21 710 | 25 936 | 54.3 % |
| vibration from a 64-entry sine table | **17 402** | **16 489** | **25 938** | **48.8 %** |

Workload: takeoff and a 20° step at one flash wait state. The roughly 26000-cycle control cost includes two atan2 calls, a square root and PIDs.

sections.title: The Real Sensor — MPU Mode
sourceHeadings: Slide 24: The Real Sensor — MPU Mode
sections.body:
**MPU mode** reads the MPU6050 IMU. **LSB** (least-significant bit) denotes a raw-count unit here. A **mutex** protects the shared bus. **SPI** is a serial bus often used for fast IMU reads.

SEL selects a real/Wokwi MPU 6050 at 0x68 sharing OLED I²C, while forced rc_arm=0 prevents motor operation. CONFIG(0x1A) DLPF_CFG bits 2:0=3 selects 44 Hz.

GYRO_CONFIG(0x1B) FS_SEL bits 4:3=0 gives ±250°/s. PWR_MGMT_1(0x6B) SLEEP bit 6=0 wakes it.

A 14-byte big-endian burst from 0x3B contains accel XYZ, temperature and gyro XYZ. Scales are 16384 LSB/g and 131 LSB/(°/s).

Mounted chip X-forward/Y-left/Z-up requires negating Y and Z to FRD. A mutex-protected 1 KB OLED flush takes about 25 ms at 400 kHz, blocking timely IMU reads and producing catch-up calls.

A real controller needs a dedicated fast IMU bus, usually SPI.

| Register / function | Width, value and bit fields |
|---|---|
| CONFIG  —  0x1A, = 3: 44 Hz | 8 = 0x03; 2:0 DLPF_CFG |
| GYRO_CONFIG  —  0x1B, left at 0: 250 deg/s | 8; 4:3 FS_SEL |
| PWR_MGMT_1  —  0x6B, = 0: awake | 8 = 0x00; 6 SLEEP |

sections.title: Telemetry for the Host
sourceHeadings: Slide 25: Telemetry for the Host
sections.body:
**Telemetry** sends measurements to another computer. A **checksum** detects damaged text. Divide a tenths-of-a-degree field by ten for degrees.

Telemetry is checksummed lesson-08 framing at 25 Hz, with integer angles in tenths of degrees and motors in thousandths because printf has no float formatting. ATT fields carry both estimate and SIM truth, setpoints, motors, arm state and Kp×100.

EST in MPU mode substitutes accel-only angles for inaccessible truth. host.py charts ATT field 2 for estimated roll and field 6 for true roll. Compare them to evaluate the filter.

25 Hz means one frame every 40 ms.

```text
$ATT,<ms>,<roll>,<pitch>,<roll set>,<pitch set>,<true roll>,<true pitch>,<M0>,<M1>,<M2>,<M3>,<armed>,<Kp x100>*CS
```

```text
python ..\08_UART_And_Python_Host\host.py --file cap.txt --chart ATT,2,-300,300
```

sections.title: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be

sections.body:
A **host** is the PC running the C model; **Wokwi** simulates hardware. Timing estimates cannot establish wiring or physical board performance.

The host ran 24 checks using the same C: default roll rise 0.20 s, settle 0.34 s, 0.3% overshoot. A 229°/s gust peaks at 11° and returns within 3° in 0.17 s.

sections.title: What Carries Forward
sourceHeadings: Slide 27: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
**GPS** means Global Positioning System. A **barometer** measures air pressure for height estimation. Add position control outside the stable, faster attitude loop.

Position control adds barometer/GPS inputs above the attitude loop in lesson 14. Cycle measurements should identify expensive paths before optimisation.

Later robots retain safety checks for stale/invalid estimates and released operator controls, along with the limitation that hidden estimation error remains hidden from failsafes. Balancing repeats attitude control with gravity making the plant unstable, motivating comparison of PID and LQR.

sections.title: Two Tiers, as in Real Drones
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: Two Tiers, as in Real Drones
sections.body:
The **MCU** (microcontroller) makes time-critical decisions; the PC sends goals and records results. Battery safety must survive ground-link loss.

Keep real-time estimation, modes, control and failsafes aboard the MCU. Python owns planning, sending, logs and scoring.

The split resembles PX 4/ArduPilot plus QGroundControl/Mission Planner; here messages use printable lesson-08 frames.

Ground messages express goals rather than time-critical wheel or motor updates.

| | On the aircraft (C, RTOS) | On the ground (Python) |
|---|---|---|
| **real world** | PX4, ArduPilot on a flight controller | QGroundControl, Mission Planner |
| **here** | `flight.c` in the `ctl` task | `host/mission.py` |
| **owns** | estimation, control loops, modes, **failsafes** | the mission, the log, the score |
| **rate** | 50 Hz, hard deadline | whenever a human clicks |
| **if the link dies** | keeps flying, decides for itself | can only watch |

sections.title: The Whole Machine
sourceHeadings: Slide 2: The Whole Machine
sections.body:
**Hz** means updates per second; **UI** means user interface. Control receives delayed sensor observations, not exact simulated position. A **lock** protects shared state.

The world runs at 100 Hz, control at 50 Hz, telemetry at 5 Hz and UI at 50 Hz with a 10 Hz OLED. control_step receives acceleration, compass, barometer and a GPS fix delayed 200 ms. Outputs request tilt, thrust and yaw rate. link accepts mission/mode intent and telemetry sends position and events. fc_lock protects shared flight state.

```c
void control_step(const sensors_t *in, actuators_t *out);
```

sections.title: Why We May Pretend the Attitude Loop Is Instant
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: Why We May Pretend the Attitude Loop Is Instant
sections.body:
**Attitude** is orientation; **bandwidth** describes response speed. **First-order lag** makes output approach its request gradually.

The attitude subsystem is approximated by an 80 ms first-order lag, updated toward commanded roll/pitch. Its 12.5 rad/s bandwidth is around 6.2 times the velocity loop.

Host wind-hold tests in the table justify this separation: at 40–80 ms true RMS stays near 1 m, but an 800 ms lag produces 3.47 m. A 5–10× bandwidth gap allows an inner controller to appear nearly instantaneous to the outer one.

| attitude lag | inner bandwidth | × velocity loop | seen RMS | true RMS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 40 ms | 25 rad/s | 12.5 × | 0.74 m | 0.99 m |
| **80 ms (this lesson)** | **12.5 rad/s** | **6.2 ×** | **0.76 m** | **1.01 m** |
| 200 ms | 5 rad/s | 2.5 × | 0.83 m | 1.06 m |
| 400 ms | 2.5 rad/s | 1.2 × | 1.30 m | 1.50 m |
| 800 ms | 1.2 rad/s | 0.6 × | 3.37 m | 3.47 m |

```c
w->roll += (r_cmd - w->roll) * dt / w->tau_att;
```

Trials use position hold in 8 m/s wind.

sections.title: The Model — a Thrust Vector, Tilted
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: The Model — a Thrust Vector, Tilted
sections.body:
Here **thrust** is force per mass and **g** is gravity. **Drag** opposes motion relative to wind. **Semi-implicit integration** updates velocity before position.

The plant accelerations are forward=T sinθ cosφ, right=T sinφ and up=T cosθ cosφ−g, yaw-rotated into world coordinates. Subtract 0.35(v−wind) drag and integrate semi-implicitly at 100 Hz.

A 25° lean sacrifices about 9% vertical thrust, so altitude must increase total thrust. Hovering in 8 m/s wind needs 2.8 m/s² horizontal acceleration to balance drag.

sections.title: Wind You Can Repeat
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: Wind You Can Repeat
sections.body:
A **seed** selects repeatable randomness. **Standard deviation** describes typical variation; **Gaussian noise** has a bell-shaped distribution.

Wind combines a knob-set 0–10 m/s steady part with each axis' random gust. The gust decays with a 2 s time constant and uses a kick σ√(2 dt/τ).

Its steady standard deviation is 30% of steady wind. xorshift32 has shifts 13,17,5 and period 2³²−1. Summing three uniforms cheaply approximates a Gaussian without log/sqrt-heavy sampling.

Seed 1 yields bit-identical host missions under 8 m/s wind.

```c
float kick = sigma * m_sqrt(2.0f * dt / GUST_TAU);
w->gust_x += -w->gust_x * dt / GUST_TAU + kick * gauss(w);
```

```c
x ^= x << 13;  x ^= x >> 17;  x ^= x << 5;
```

sections.title: A Battery That Knows How Hard You Fly
sourceHeadings: Slide 6: A Battery That Knows How Hard You Fly
sections.body:
**Load** is thrust/gravity. **RTL** returns home; critical battery requires local landing to avoid extra travel.

Battery drain scales with load^(3/2), where load=thrust/g. At hover it drains 0.35 percentage points/s, about 4.8 minutes from full.

Climbs and wind lean increase demand. Host mission finish levels are 79.3% still and 76.6% in wind.

Low battery at 25% requests RTL. Critical 10% requests immediate landing.

Faster flight is not automatically lower energy flight.

| | value |
|---|---|
| hover, still air | 0.35 %/s → about 4.8 minutes |
| default mission, still air | 100 → **79.3 %** |
| same, 8 m/s wind | 100 → **76.6 %** (fighting the wind costs) |
| `BAT_LOW` 25 % | → **RTL** (the related topic) |
| `BAT_CRIT` 10 % | → **LAND where you are** |

```c
float load = w->thrust / GRAVITY;
w->battery -= w->drain * load * m_sqrt(load) * dt;
```

sections.title: Sensors That Lie a Little
sourceHeadings: Slide 7: Sensors That Lie a Little
sections.body:
**Bias** is persistent offset; **RMS** (root mean square) summarizes typical magnitude. **GPS** (Global Positioning System) fixes can share errors across samples.

Acceleration is supplied in world axes with gravity removed. The attitude layer must perform that transform first.

The table lists sensor errors. Shared GPS wander is about 0.65 m RMS on the host.

Filtering cannot distinguish it from a real slowly moving position. A 0.03 m/s² acceleration bias accumulates into velocity and position error.

| Sensor | Rate | Error modelled | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| accelerometer (world frame) | 50 Hz | 0.2 m/s² noise, **0.03 m/s² bias** | integrate it and it drifts |
| compass (yaw) | 50 Hz | 0.01 rad | small |
| barometer | 50 Hz | 0.2 m noise | jumpy altitude |
| **GPS** | **10 Hz** | **200 ms late**; 0.4 m slow wander + 0.1 m jitter | the hard one |

sections.title: The 200 ms Problem
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: The 200 ms Problem
sections.body:
A **historical ring buffer** stores recent estimates, reusing slots at its end. Compare delayed fixes against estimates of the same past instant.

A GPS fix describes the aircraft ten 20 ms steps ago. Compare it with that historical estimate, then shift current and stored position estimates by the correction.

The ring index wraps modulo FC_HIST. Comparing the past fix with present position falsely attributes 0.8 m travel at 4 m/s over 0.2 s to estimator error.

Host delayed fusion lowers RMS from 1.08 to 0.69 m in still air, and 0.98 to 0.68 m in wind.

| | still air | 8 m/s wind |
|---|---|---|
| estimate error, compared with the past (this code) | **0.69 m** RMS | **0.68 m** |
| compared with now (`GPS_LAG_STEPS 0`) | 1.08 m | 0.98 m |
| the GPS's own slow error, for scale | 0.65 m | 0.64 m |

```c
uint8_t then = (uint8_t)((now + FC_HIST - GPS_LAG_STEPS) % FC_HIST);
float rx = s->gps_x - fc.hx[then];
...
for (unsigned k = 0; k < FC_HIST; k++) { fc.hx[k] += a * rx; fc.hy[k] += a * ry; }
```

sections.title: Cascaded Control
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Cascaded Control
sections.body:
The **cascade** converts position error→speed→acceleration→tilt/thrust. **P** is proportional action; **PI** adds integral error.

Position P (KP_POS=1.0) requests velocity bounded by HOLD_V or CRUISE. Velocity PI (KP_VEL=2.0, KI=0.6) requests acceleration bounded by g tan(TILT).

At 25°, that cap is 4.57 m/s². Tilt conversion feeds the 80 ms attitude lag.

The approximate response bandwidth decreases toward the outer loops: 12.5, 2.4 and 1 rad/s. Each layer limits demand.

sections.title: From Acceleration to Tilt
sourceHeadings: Slide 12: From Acceleration to Tilt

sections.title: The Integral Term Is a Wind Gauge
sourceHeadings: Slide 13: The Integral Term Is a Wind Gauge
sections.body:
**P** reacts to current error; **I** accumulates it, retaining wind correction after error becomes small.

Velocity integral provides a steady acceleration to cancel wind while position error becomes small. In 8 m/s wind, proportional-only prediction is 2.8/(1×2)=1.4 m downwind offset.

Host sees 1.26 m. KI=0.6 lowers mean offset to 0.23 m and RMS to 1.01 m, versus 1.59 m without I.

Dividing integral acceleration by drag coefficient estimates wind: host estimate 7.1 m/s for true 8.0, with 12.9° lean. The comparison uses a 30 s hold.

Drag coefficient is 0.35 s⁻¹.

| | mean offset downwind | true RMS error |
|---|---|---|
| `KI_VEL` = 0.6 (default) | **0.23 m** | 1.01 m |
| `KI_VEL` = 0 | **1.26 m** | 1.59 m |

sections.title: You Cannot Hold Better Than You Can See
sourceHeadings: Slide 14: You Cannot Hold Better Than You Can See
sections.body:
The controller sees estimated position; the simulator also exposes truth. **RMS** error magnitudes need not add like signed instantaneous errors.

Separate three errors: seen=estimate−setpoint, blind=truth−estimate, true=truth−setpoint. Host 30 s wind hold gives 0.76,0.67,1.01 m RMS respectively.

Instantaneous signed errors add; RMS also depends on correlation. Tuning controls seen error.

GPS wander shared across fixes limits blind error. POS reports belief while TRU exposes model truth for evaluation.

GPS slow wander itself is about 0.65 m RMS.

| error | RMS | what it is | who can fix it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **seen** (estimate − setpoint) | **0.76 m** | what the controller knows it is missing by | **tuning** |
| **blind** (truth − estimate) | **0.67 m** | what the estimator gets wrong | better sensors |
| **true** (truth − setpoint) | **1.01 m** | what a person on the ground would see | both |

Trials use 8 m/s wind with gusts.

sections.title: Flight Modes — One State Machine
sourceHeadings: Slide 15: Flight Modes — One State Machine
sections.body:
A **state machine** defines modes and transitions: **TAKEOFF** rises, **HOLD** stays, **MISSION** follows goals, **RTL** returns and **LAND** descends. **EVT** logs transitions.

Modes are DISARMED, TAKEOFF, HOLD, MISSION, RTL and LAND. A/ARM begins takeoff.

Absent mission leads to hold and a loaded mission to mission flight. A/SEL selects hold, B requests RTL, mission completion returns, and battery/fence events override ordinary transitions.

Landing requires low and still for 1.5 s. All transitions go through enter(), which logs reason with EVT and installs a defined stay-here setpoint.

RTL climbs to at least 10 m, flies home without descending en route, then lands at home.

sourceHeadings: Slide 19: Checked Before It Flies

**ACK** acknowledges; **ERR** rejects. **PREARM** means a starting condition remains unmet.

Validate every waypoint against the fence before mission start. An empty mission or missing intermediate index returns ERR, EMPTY.

A waypoint 60 m away with a 50 m fence returns ERR, FENCE. A valid start enters TAKEOFF.

sections.title: MAVLink-lite
sourceHeadings: Slide 20: MAVLink-lite
sections.body:
**MAVLink** is a drone messaging protocol. **ACK** confirms reception; **CRC** (cyclic redundancy check) detects damaged data.

MAVLink-lite retains mission/parameter/mode/ACK concepts using checksummed text. Coordinates are integer decimetres relative to home.

Real MISSION_ITEM_INT local positions use metres×10⁴ in int 32. The table maps each simplified frame to real message/command IDs.

Real MAVLink uses binary CRC-16 and vehicle-driven item requests. Here mission.py waits for each ACK and retries up to three times, with no upload handshake.

Radio loss would require stronger transaction handling.

sections.title: A Parser That Trusts Nothing
sourceHeadings: Slide 21: A Parser That Trusts Nothing
sections.body:
A **checksum** detects transport damage. Commands also need valid field counts, complete numeric syntax, lengths and ranges.

Validate checksum, refuse bodies over 63 bytes without truncation, check command field count, parse each complete numeric string, check ranges, then call flight logic. Valid ranges are waypoint 0–15, horizontal ±1 km and altitude 0–200 m.

Mission start rechecks the fence. Host round-trip results: 9/9 normal frames accepted, 0/9 bit-corrupted frames accepted, 11/11 malformed checksummed frames rejected, and all five downloaded waypoints equal the file.

|---|---|
| the 9 frames of `default.mission` | **9 / 9** acknowledged `OK` |
| each with one bit flipped | **0 / 9** got through |
| 11 well-checksummed but malformed frames | **11 / 11** refused |

sections.title: `mission.py` — Plan, Send, Score
sourceHeadings: Slide 22: `mission.py` — Plan, Send, Score
sections.body:
**TRU** reports simulation truth; **POS** reports estimated position. Score actual motion using TRU.

mission.py can print frames, generate a 40×30 survey with its lawnmower options, upload over rfc 2217://localhost:4000 and log, or score captured telemetry/race output. Real vehicles cannot send perfect truth.

Host C at 50 Hz and Python at 5 Hz agree closely: completion 60.96/61.00 s, cross-track 2.06/2.07 m, worst waypoint 1.75/1.74 m and landing 0.44/0.45 m. Core tooling is stdlib-only.

Live --port needs pyserial.

```text
python host\mission.py host\default.mission             frames to paste into Wokwi
python host\mission.py --gen lawnmower 40 30 4 8         a survey pattern, as a file
python host\mission.py my.mission --port rfc2217://localhost:4000 --log flight.log
python host\mission.py --score capture.txt --race        score any captured flight
```

sections.title: Five Tasks, Three Locks
sourceHeadings: Slide 23: Five Tasks, Three Locks
sections.body:
A **task** owns specified work. **Deadlock** means tasks wait forever for each other’s locks; consistent lock order prevents cycles.

The task/priority/period table defines world, ctl, link, tel and UI ownership. link alone may hold two locks, always fc_lock then world_lock. This prevents lock cycles.

UI copies state quickly then releases its lock before the roughly 25 ms OLED flush. Four actuator words cross in a brief interrupt-masked copy.

Physics stays highest priority because delayed display or serial work must not distort world timing.

| Task | Prio | Period | Touches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `world` | 5 | 10 ms | world (`world_lock`), `act` (critical section) |
| `ctl` | 4 | 20 ms | world → `sensors_t`, flight state (`fc_lock`) |
| `link` | 3 | per byte | flight state; world via `$PARAM,WIND` |
| `tel` | 2 | 200 ms | flight state, then the truth |
| `ui` | 1 | 20 ms | flight state, world (knob); OLED, alone |

sections.title: The Ground Station on the OLED
sourceHeadings: Slide 24: The Ground Station on the OLED

A **breadcrumb** marks an earlier position. Map pixels represent distance; the side panel reports mode, height and battery numerically.

The host rendered ui.c and oled.c pixel for pixel at 40 s of the windy mission. The map scale is 1.6 m/pixel, showing a dotted 50 m fence, waypoint crosses with a box on the active one, dotted planned legs, 0.5 s breadcrumbs and a heading-marked aircraft dot.

sections.title: What It Costs — Flash and RAM
sourceHeadings: Slide 25: What It Costs — Flash and RAM
sections.body:
**Flash** holds code; **RAM** holds data and stacks. A **high-water mark** is deepest observed stack use, unlike a static estimate.

Initial FLASH/RAM were 30736/12576 B, exceeding RAM at 102%. Per-task stack sizing saved about 2 KB, shared math copies saved 720 B flash and replacing streamed stdio with vsnprintf+_write saved 1860 B.

Final build is 27428 B flash (83.7%) and 10520 B RAM (85.6%), zero warnings in the source build. Link's deepest formatting chain is about 0.9 KB of a 1.25 KB stack.

Confirm static stack estimates with target high-water measurements.

| Change | Saved | Why |
|---|---|---|
| task stacks 384 → 160–320 words, sized per task | ~2 KB RAM | a 384-word stack for a task that needs 100 is RAM nobody uses |
| `fm.c`: sin, cos, atan2, sqrt compiled **once** | **720 B** flash | `static inline` gave each of four files its own copies |
| `say()` = `vsnprintf` + `_write`, no stdio stream | **1860 B** flash | `printf`/`fputs` to `stdout` drag in buffering, flushing, `malloc` |

sections.title: What Carries Forward
sourceHeadings: Slide 28: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
Bounded control and independent evaluation transfer to hardware, where independent position measurements can replace simulation truth.

Later robots reuse bounded cascades, line cross-track correction and Python intent planning with onboard execution. Log both belief and truth where a simulator provides truth.

Keep failsafes ahead of pilot requests; measure CPU/RAM before assuming the app fits.

The balancing example shows why a slow inner loop cannot always be abstracted away.

sections.title: Board connections and controls
sourceHeadings: The Board: This Lesson's Pins
sections.body:
**ADC** converts voltage to numbers. **USART** uses **TX/RX** (transmit/receive); **I²C** uses **SDA/SCL** (data/clock). **OLED** is the display; **GND** is ground and **3V3** is 3.3 V.

Nucleo-C031C6/MB1717 exposes outer ST morpho double rows and inner Arduino A0–A5/D0–D15 rows. Some signals share labels, for example PA5/D13.

Use the actual connected header position. Power is 3V3 and GND.

PA0/PA1 are joystick ADC IN0/IN1. PA4 is ADC IN4 for the knob.

PA2/PA3 USART2 TX/RX. PA6 TIM3_CH1 buzzer.

PB8/PB9 I²C1 SCL/SDA for OLED at 0x3C. PB4/PB5 buttons A/B and PB3 stick select.

A starts/stops. B changes track.

SEL switches manual/automatic. Knob sets speed.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads levels; **MODER** selects mode; **AFR** selects alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal. Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly.

sourceHeadings: Slide 1: The Race
sections.body:
A **checksum** detects damaged result text. The knob requests straight-line speed; corners may require slowing.

The joystick chooses OVAL/S-BENDS/HAIRPINS/FIGURE-8 before A starts. A again returns to line, B advances track and SEL selects manual driving.

The knob commands straight speed 0–2000 mm/s. Shell commands tune gains/noise/failures.

**Software-in-the-loop (SITL)** runs controller code with modeled sensors and motors. The world judges laps from true position.

SITL separates a 200 Hz world with motors, tyres, reflectance, encoders and true lap judge from a 100 Hz controller. Only the controller would ship on a real robot.

UI/shell/display inspect state without steering. Real sensor and motor drivers can replace world.c.

sections.title: Model 1 — Differential Drive
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: Model 1 — Differential Drive
sections.body:
**Differential drive** uses two independently driven wheels. **Yaw rate** measures how fast the heading turns.

With a 100 mm wheelbase, forward speed is (wl+wr)/2 and yaw rate is (wr−wl)/100 in rad/s for mm/s wheel units. A faster right wheel turns left.

The seven-sensor bar is 70 mm ahead of the axle and its offset later gives heading-error lead. Wheel-speed difference steers.

```text
v     = (wl + wr) / 2           forward speed, mm/s
omega = (wr - wl) / 100 mm      turn rate, rad/s: right wheel faster = turn left
```

sections.title: Encoders Count Wheels, Not Ground
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Encoders Count Wheels, Not Ground
sections.body:
An **encoder** counts wheel movement; **odometry** estimates motion from it. **Slip** breaks the rotation-to-ground-distance relationship.

Encoders integrate wheel travel regardless of slip. With 360 ticks/revolution and 16 mm wheel radius, scale is 360/(2π×16)≈3.58 ticks/mm.

During sideways slide the wheels keep rotating, so inferred ground distance is wrong. This line controller uses reflectance and ignores encoders.

The contract retains them for odometry exercises and the next navigation lesson.

```c
    world.dist_l += world.wl * dt;
    world.dist_r += world.wr * dt;
```

sections.title: Model 4 — The Sensor Bar
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: Model 4 — The Sensor Bar
sections.body:
**Sensor pitch** is neighbour spacing. **Interpolation** uses partial-coverage readings to estimate tape position between sensors.

The track is 19 mm-wide tape and seven sensors are spaced 13 mm. A finite 4 mm sensor spot gives partial coverage near an edge rather than a binary jump.

Coverage is clamped from distance to the nearest taped centreline. Reflectance becomes clamp(100+800×coverage+ambient+noise,0,1000).

```c
        world.cov[k] = f_clamp((TAPE_HALF_MM + SPOT_MM - dmin) / (2.0f * SPOT_MM), 0.0f, 1.0f);
```

sections.title: Finding the Tape Cheaply
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: Finding the Tape Cheaply
sections.body:
A **bounding box** encloses an object in a rectangle. **Soft-float** implements floating-point arithmetic in software without an FPU.

Finding tape exactly across 111 segments for seven sensors at 200 Hz would need about 155000 soft-float distances/s. Integer bounding boxes around the bar reject far segments with four comparisons.

Host average candidates are 2.8–3.7 per step, at most six, out of 70–110. Both FIGURE-8 branches survive at a crossing, producing a dark cross naturally.

The true lap judge instead searches segments −4…6 near previous progress to preserve branch identity.

```c
        if (ibx + reach < lox || ibx - reach > hix || iby + reach < loy || iby - reach > hiy) { continue; }
        cand[nc++] = i;
```

sections.title: Tracks Are Turtle Programs
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Tracks Are Turtle Programs

Fixed simulation steps do not establish target deadlines: late MCU steps make model lap time differ from wall-clock time.

Source host checks pass for closure, five-lap defaults, speed/gain/filter/fault sweeps, repeatability and the actual view framebuffer. Source firmware builds warning-free at 26920 B flash/9352 B RAM.

sourceHeadings: Slide 28: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
Explicit sensor/command contracts keep controllers testable when simulated devices become real.

The same control_step seam carries IMUs/motors for drones, tilt/torque for balancers or line/wheel commands here. A highest-priority world with truth-based judge supports repeatable host trials.

Navigation adds obstacles/planning, and sumo adds two controllers in one world. Real robot telemetry can preserve comparable fields, although perfect world truth then needs separate measurement.

sections.title: Board connections and controls
sourceHeadings: The Board: This Lesson's Pins
sections.body:
**ADC** converts joystick/knob voltage to numbers. **USART** uses **TX/RX** (transmit/receive); **I²C** uses **SDA/SCL** (data/clock). **OLED** is the display; **GND** is ground and **3V3** is 3.3 V.

Nucleo-C031C6/MB1717 exposes outer ST morpho double rows and inner Arduino A0–A5/D0–D15 rows. Some signals share labels, for example PA5/D13.

Use the actual connected header position. Power is 3V3 and GND.

PA0/PA1 are joystick ADC IN0/IN1. PA4 is ADC IN4 for the knob.

PA2/PA3 USART2 TX/RX. PA6 TIM3_CH1 buzzer.

PB8/PB9 I²C1 SCL/SDA for OLED at 0x3C. PB4/PB5 buttons A/B and PB3 stick select.

A starts/restarts. B changes level.

SEL reveals true walls. Knob sets speed.

PA5 indicates arrival. PA5 is the onboard LD4 output.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads levels; **MODER** selects mode; **AFR** selects alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug. A **pull-up** holds an open input high.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

PA5 is output for LD4. Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal.

Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly. Buttons/select use pull-ups.

sections.title: The Problem in One Picture
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: The Problem in One Picture
sections.body:
**Localisation** estimates **pose** (position and heading). An **FPU** is a floating-point unit; this MCU has none. **Reactive safety** responds to current danger.

Navigation couples localisation, mapping and planning: bad pose places sensed walls in the wrong cells and a bad map misleads the path planner. The screen distinguishes real position from estimate and discovered walls from unseen ones.

The 48 MHz no-FPU target has to execute all three layers within 12 KB RAM, and safety still needs immediate sensor-based decisions when the plan is wrong.

sections.title: The World Is a Little Wrong, on Purpose
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: The World Is a Little Wrong, on Purpose
sections.body:
**Bias** is fixed offset; **noise** varies by sample. **Odometry** estimates motion from wheels, which can turn while the body is blocked.

Differences between assumed and true plant parameters are deliberate: true wheel scales 1.010/0.995, wheelbase 61.5 instead of 60 mm, motor τ0.1 s, gyro bias 0.004 rad/s with 0.002 rad/s noise. Beams sample every 25 mm, range noise is ±(3 mm+1.5%), and 1/64 echoes are missing.

Walls can stop the body while wheels corrupt odometry. Thin geometry between ray samples may be invisible.

| Reality | What it does to the robot |
|---|---|
| motors lag 0.1 s | it cannot stop or turn instantly |
| wheels 1.0% / 0.5% off the datasheet, wheelbase 61.5 not 60 | odometry **drifts** |
| gyro bias 4 mrad/s, noise 2 mrad/s | integrate it raw and heading walks 14° a minute |
| beam sampled every 25 mm | a corner thinner than a step along the beam is **never seen** |
| ±(3 mm + 1.5%) noise; 1 echo in 64 lost | the map gets ghosts and holes |
| a wall stops the body, **not the wheels** | a collision corrupts the odometry too |

```c
#define SCALE_L        1.010f
#define SCALE_R        0.995f
#define WHEELBASE_TRUE 61.5f
#define MOTOR_TAU_S    0.10f
#define GYRO_BIAS      0.004f
#define RAY_STEP_MM    25.0f
#define DROPOUT_MASK   63u
```

sections.title: The Layered Robot
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: The Layered Robot
sections.body:
**Deliberative control** reasons from stored knowledge; **reactive control** uses current measurements. Their disagreements require recovery rules.

The chain is estimate→map→plan→follow→protect. Deliberative layers reason from a persistent uncertain map.

Reactive protection acts on current ranges and may override any planned command. This resembles subsumption and a three-layer robot architecture, or emergency braking below a driver.

An explicit disagreement policy is needed so a blocked plan does not cause endless standstill. Historical models behind this separation include Brooks subsumption (1986) and Gat three-layer architecture (1998).

sections.body:
An **occupancy grid** accumulates evidence that cells are occupied, free or unknown. Repeated clear observations can remove a weak wall.

Store signed occupancy evidence in int 8 cells (448 B): clear traversed cells by−1 and add+3 at an echo hit 30 mm beyond measured range, clamp−4…+6. v≥2 means occupied, v≤−1 free, otherwise unknown. One hit can establish a wall.

Three clearing passes remove it. A no-echo 600 mm reading clears only 450 mm because dropout is indistinguishable from empty space.

Placing hits behind echoes avoids marking the preceding free cell from noise.

sections.title: Layer 3 — A* in Four Lines
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: Layer 3 — A* in Four Lines
sections.body:
**A\*** scores candidates with **f=g+h**: spent cost **g** plus remaining-cost **heuristic h**. **Octile distance** accounts for straight and diagonal steps.

A* picks lowest f=g+h, expands eight neighbours and reconstructs parents when it reaches goal. Straight cost 10, diagonal 14 and destination-cell penalties comprise g.

Octile h=10 max(dx, dy)+4 min(dx, dy) never overestimates an empty-grid route. A diagonal is forbidden if either adjacent side cell is wall.

Integer-only astar.c correctly exhausts 335 reachable cells for a sealed goal and 0 for a goal inside a wall.

```text
open = {start};  g(start) = 0
repeat:  take the open cell with the lowest  f = g + h
         if it is the goal: follow the parents back - done
         close it; offer each of its 8 neighbours a cheaper g
```

sections.title: Layer 4 — Pure Pursuit
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: Layer 4 — Pure Pursuit
sections.body:
**Pure pursuit** follows a lookahead **carrot**. **Curvature** is turning per unit travel. Guard tiny distances and blocked sightlines.

Pure pursuit chooses a 220 mm lookahead carrot and curvature 2 sinα/L, then ω=v×curvature. Restrict carrot to line-of-sight through the map so it cannot lie behind a wall at a bend.

Skip a near-coincident carrot: a 2 mm target caused noisy bearing and 120 s spinning in the original host test. Path followers need geometry guards as well as the nominal formula.

sourceHeadings: The Board: This Lesson's Pins
sections.body:
**ADC** converts voltage to numbers. **USART** uses **TX/RX** (transmit/receive); **I²C** uses **SDA/SCL** (data/clock). **OLED** is the display; **GND** is ground and **3V3** is 3.3 V.

Nucleo-C031C6/MB1717 exposes outer ST morpho double rows and inner Arduino A0–A5/D0–D15 rows. Some signals share labels, for example PA5/D13.

Use the actual connected header position. Power is 3V3 and GND.

PA0/PA1 are joystick ADC IN0/IN1. PA4 is ADC IN4 for the knob.

PA2/PA3 USART2 TX/RX. PA6 TIM3_CH1 buzzer.

PB8/PB9 I²C1 SCL/SDA for OLED at 0x3C. PB4/PB5 buttons A/B and PB3 stick select.

A stands up. B applies a push.

SEL advances controller. Knob sets payload.

Vertical stick sets driving speed.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads levels; **MODER** selects mode; **AFR** selects alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal. Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly.

sections.title: A Robot Inside the Chip
sourceHeadings: Slide 1: A Robot Inside the Chip
sections.body:
An **inverted pendulum** falls away from upright unless corrected. **RTOS** means real-time operating system; its tasks schedule simulation, control and display.

The world solves a wheeled inverted pendulum at 1 kHz. Control estimates state and chooses PID-tilt, cascade or LQR at 200 Hz.

Driver/UI runs 50 Hz and display 10 Hz, alongside shell on the RTOS. A stands it up, B applies a push and knob changes payload.

Only the world stores true tilt. Controllers receive noisy sensors.

This is actual portable controller C against a model, with simulation also consuming target CPU.

sections.title: The Model — a Pendulum on Wheels
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: The Model — a Pendulum on Wheels
sections.body:
**Tilt/translation coupling** means each affects the other. **Torque** turns the wheels and applies opposite reaction torque to the body.

The equations couple horizontal acceleration and tilt acceleration through MLcosθ. θ=0 is upright and positive leans forward. Motor torque acts between wheel and body, with reaction−τ in the tilt equation.

Gravity MgLsinθ destabilises upright. Accelerating wheels forward catches a forward fall.

External push F contributes both translation and a moment FLcosθ. The table-free coupled equations below define the plant.

```text
(M + mw + Iw/r²) x''  +  M L cosθ θ''  =  τ/r + M L sinθ θ'² − b x' + F
M L cosθ        x''   +  (I + M L²) θ'' =  M g L sinθ − τ + F L cosθ
```

sections.title: The Numbers — `params.h`, One Source of Truth
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: The Numbers — `params.h`, One Source of Truth
sections.body:
**Inertia** resists rotational acceleration. **RMS** (root mean square) summarizes typical magnitude. A **mounting error** is a physical sensor angular offset.

params.h defines body 0.80 kg, centre 0.10 m, inertia 0.0045 kg·m². Wheels 0.10 kg, radius 35 mm.

Two motors k 0.20 N·m/A and 4Ω. Supply 7.4 V.

Knob payload up to 0.6 kg at 0.20 m. Sensors have gyro 0.010 rad/s RMS plus 0.005 bias, acceleration 0.30 m/s² RMS,1° mounting error and 1440 counts/rev.

World/controller periods 1/5 ms. lqr.py parses ordered #define expressions, removes float suffixes and evaluates with no builtins so design and model share parameter values.

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| body | 0.80 kg, CoM 10 cm above the axle, I = 0.0045 kg m² | `BOT_MB BOT_L BOT_IB` |
| wheels | 0.10 kg, r = 35 mm | `BOT_MW BOT_R` |
| motors | 2 × (k = 0.20 N m/A, R = 4 Ω), at the wheel | `MOT_N MOT_K MOT_RES` |
| supply | 7.4 V (two lithium cells) | `VBAT` |
| payload | up to 0.6 kg at 20 cm (the knob) | `PAY_MAX PAY_H` |
| sensors | gyro ±0.010 rad/s rms + 0.005 bias; accel ±0.30 m/s² rms; IMU 1° crooked; 1440 counts/rev | |
| timing | world 1 ms, controller 5 ms | `WORLD_DT CTRL_DT` |

```python
expr = re.sub(r"(\d)[fF]\b", r"\1", m.group(2))   # 0.80f -> 0.80
names[m.group(1)] = float(eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}}, dict(names)))
```

sections.title: The Motor Fights Back
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: The Motor Fights Back
sections.body:
**Back-EMF** is generated voltage opposing motor drive. **Stall torque** occurs at zero speed; **no-load speed** occurs without external load.

Relative motor speed is xdot/r−θdot. Torque is motor count times [k(u−kωrel)/R−motor damping×ωrel].

Each motor stalls at 0.37 N·m, both 0.74 N·m or 21 N at tyre. No-load 37 rad/s corresponds 1.3 m/s.

At 1 m/s only about 1.7 V remains for torque. The plant clips to 7.4 V and counts clipped steps.

| | per motor | both |
|---|---|---|
| stall torque, 7.4 V | k V / R = 0.37 N m | 0.74 N m → 21 N at the tyre |
| no-load speed | V / k = 37 rad/s | 1.3 m/s |

```c
float w_rel = w->xd * (1.0f / BOT_R) - w->thd;
float tau = MOT_N * (MOT_K * (u - MOT_K * w_rel) / MOT_RES - MOT_B * w_rel);
```

sections.title: Linearised — What `lqr.py` Sees
sourceHeadings: Slide 7: Linearised — What `lqr.py` Sees
sections.body:
**Linearisation** approximates relationships by local slopes near upright. A **pole** describes mode growth/decay; a positive real pole means instability.

Linearise upright with sinθ≈θ, cosθ≈1 and squared-rate term neglected. State order is [x, xdot, θ, θdot], input volts.

A and B below come from params.h. Poles+7.04,0,−5.68,−70.41 s⁻¹ represent tipping growth, free position, velocity decay and fast motor damping.

Positive tilt grows e-fold in 1/7.04≈142 ms. The 5 ms controller samples about 28 times within that growth time.

| pole | meaning |
|---|---|
| **+7.04** | **falling over**: a tilt multiplies by e every 142 ms |
| 0 | position: nothing in physics cares where the robot is |
| −5.68 | speed decaying through back-EMF and friction |
| −70.4 | the motor's own fast electrical-mechanical damping |

```text
[    0.0000     1.0000     0.0000     0.0000 ]   [   0.0000 ]
  [    0.0000   -54.8639   -11.4674     1.9162 ]   [   7.9843 ]
  [    0.0000     0.0000     0.0000     1.0000 ]   [   0.0000 ]
  [    0.0000   405.9864   136.1753   -14.1840 ]   [ -59.0998 ]
open-loop poles (1/s): +7.04+0.00j, +0.00+0.00j, -5.68+0.00j, -70.41+0.00j
  the unstable one, +7.04/s: an uncontrolled tilt grows e-fold every 142 ms
```

sections.title: Sensors That Lie
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Sensors That Lie
sections.body:
**Specific force** includes support and motion felt by the sensor. Integrated gyro bias drifts; **quantisation** gives discrete count-sized readings.

Gyro rate integrates a 0.005 rad/s bias indefinitely. Accelerometer measures specific force, not angle: standing still atan 2(−af, au) gives tilt, but forward acceleration a shifts it by roughly−a/g.

Encoder quantisation is about 0.15 mm/count. The 1° crooked IMU introduces a shared offset a complementary filter cannot detect.

| sensor | what it measures | how it lies |
|---|---|---|
| **gyro** | θ̇, the tilt *rate* | + 0.005 rad/s bias, + noise. Integrate it and the bias grows into an error **forever** |
| **accelerometer** | specific force: acceleration *minus gravity*, in body axes | noise — and it **cannot tell leaning from accelerating** |
| **encoder** | wheel angle *relative to the body*, in whole counts | quantised: 1 count = 0.15 mm of travel |

```c
float af = fx * c - fy * s;
```

sections.title: The Complementary Filter
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: The Complementary Filter
sections.body:
A **complementary filter** weights gyro prediction and accelerometer correction with **alpha**. **Tau** describes correction response time.

The filter estimatesθ=α(θ+gyro×dt)+(1−α)θacc. At alpha 0.98 and dt 0.005 s, tau is 0.245 s.

Gyro supplies fast changes; acceleration anchors long-term tilt. Host LQR tests give 1.19° RMS over 10 s from 6°, versus 3.8° for gyro-only after 30 s.

Accelerometer-only falls. Test durations/initial conditions differ, so the rows are evidence for failure modes rather than an identical-run sweep.

| α | estimator | run | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.98 | complementary | 10 s, from 6° | **1.19° rms**, upright |
| 1.00 | gyro only | 30 s, from upright | 3.8° rms, still upright — but the bias error only grows |
| 0.00 | accelerometer only | 10 s, from upright | **fell** |

```c
est.th = alpha * (est.th + in->gyro * CTRL_DT) + (1.0f - alpha) * est.th_acc;
```

sections.title: PID on Tilt — It Stands. Then It Leaves.
sourceHeadings: Slide 12: PID on Tilt — It Stands. Then It Leaves.
sections.body:
Holding tilt alone leaves position uncontrolled. Sensor offset and back-EMF can drive sustained travel into voltage saturation.

Tilt PID uses gains 150,50,4 and integral clamped±0.1. It has no position reference.

Host no-command flight balances while travelling, then falls at 7.8 s and 3.3 m. Back-EMF needs voltage for motion.

Tilt-only control creates voltage through lean, but lean requires acceleration, escalating speed until voltage saturates. A 1° crooked IMU can start this chain even when its displayed tilt is zero.

```c
integ = f_clamp(integ + est.th * CTRL_DT, -0.1f, 0.1f);
u = TILT_KP * est.th + TILT_KI * integ + TILT_KD * in->gyro;
```

sections.title: The Eigenvalues Agree
sourceHeadings: Slide 13: The Eigenvalues Agree
sections.body:
A **discrete pole** inside the unit circle decays; one at unity does not. Slow stable motion may still exceed room or motor limits.

Discrete closed-loop poles must lie inside the unit circle. Host PD 150/0/4 has z 1.00152 (3.29 s growth), lower 25/0/2 has 1.00847 (0.59 s).

Adding I 150/50/4 yields position pole 1 and slow 0.99992±0.00035 j swing of 88.9 s. Integral tilt acts indirectly like accumulated velocity correction, but does not restore position.

```text
$ python lqr.py --pid 150,0,4
  +1.00152+0.00000j   |z| = 1.00152   UNSTABLE: grows e-fold every 3.29 s
$ python lqr.py --pid 25,0,2
  +1.00847-0.00000j   |z| = 1.00847   UNSTABLE: grows e-fold every 0.59 s
$ python lqr.py --pid 150,50,4
  +1.00000+0.00000j   |z| = 1.00000   = 1: position - nothing pulls it back (drift)
  +0.99992-0.00035j   |z| = 0.99992   slow swing, period 88.9 s
```

sections.title: The Cascade Is State Feedback in Disguise
sourceHeadings: Slide 15: The Cascade Is State Feedback in Disguise
sections.body:
Expanding an unclipped cascade gives weighted **state feedback**. Similar gains do not imply identical design or limiting behaviour.

Expanding unsaturated cascade producesu=25θ+2θdot+5(x−xref)+15(xdot−vref). These four feedback magnitudes closely match LQR 5.12,15.26,21.26,2.46.

Cascade gain products were tuned to approximate state-feedback gains; design and clamp behaviour still differ.

| | x (V/m) | ẋ (V per m/s) | θ (V/rad) | θ̇ (V per rad/s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cascade | 5.0 | 15.0 | 25.0 | 2.0 |
| **LQR** | **5.12** | **15.26** | **21.26** | **2.46** |

```text
u = KP·θ + KD·θ̇ + KP·KPX·(x − x_ref) + KP·KVX·(ẋ − v_ref)      (inside the clamp)
  = 25·θ + 2·θ̇ + 5.0·(x − x_ref) + 15·(ẋ − v_ref)
```

sections.title: LQR — Say What You Want, Get the Gains
sourceHeadings: Slide 16: LQR — Say What You Want, Get the Gains
sections.body:
**LQR** minimizes squared state errors weighted by **Q** and squared command weighted by **R**. Their relative weights determine the optimum.

Minimize summed future cost xᵀQx+uRu.

Default diag(30,2,50,0.5), R 1. Increasing position weight presses harder to return, tilt weight promotes upright, rate weight smooths tilt motion and R restrains voltage.

Scaling both Q/R equally leaves K unchanged. Bryson's initial rule uses 1/(largest acceptable error)², then measurements refine priorities.

| raise | and the robot... |
|---|---|
| `q_x` | holds its spot harder — leans harder to get back |
| `q_θ` | stands straighter — spends volts to do it |
| `q_ω` | moves its tilt more gently |
| `R` | is lazier with the motor: softer, smaller voltages, more wander |

```text
J = Σ  ( xᵀ Q x  +  u R u )        over all future steps
       k
Q = diag(q_x, q_v, q_θ, q_ω)       how much each error HURTS
R                                   how much each volt COSTS
```

sections.title: The Riccati Equation, by Iteration
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: The Riccati Equation, by Iteration
sections.body:
**Zero-order hold** keeps voltage constant between updates. The **Riccati equation** computes future-cost matrix **P** and feedback gains **K**.

lqr.py derives continuous A/B, discretises zero-order held 5 ms voltage through an augmented matrix exponential, iterates the discrete Riccati update and computesK=(R+BᵀPB)⁻¹BᵀPA. One actuator makes the inverse a scalar division.

Its Taylor/scaling-and-squaring expm and small matrix helpers need only Python stdlib. The source host solution converged in 2729 iterations before checking stability and emitting C gain constants.

```python
A, B   = linear_model(p)              # the related topic, from params.h
Ad, Bd = discretise(A, B, dt)         # zero-order hold: exp([[A, B], [0, 0]] dt)
for k in range(iters):                # P <- Q + A'PA - A'PB (R + B'PB)^-1 B'PA
    ...
K = (R + B'PB)^-1 B'PA
```

sections.title: The Firmware — Five Tasks, One Owner Each
sourceHeadings: Slide 20: The Firmware — Five Tasks, One Owner Each
sections.body:

sections.title: Timing It — TIM14 as a Stopwatch
sourceHeadings: Slide 21: Timing It — TIM14 as a Stopwatch
sections.body:
A **prescaler** divides the timer clock. An **update event** loads its buffered value before timing begins.

M0+ lacks DWT CYCCNT. Enable TIM14 through APBENR2 bit 15, PSC 47 makes 48 MHz/48=1 MHz, ARR 0xFFFF gives 65.536 ms wrap and CEN bit 0 starts it.

EGR.UG bit 0 loads the buffered prescaler immediately. Otherwise initial ticks use the wrong frequency.

PSC/ARR/CNT are 16-bit fields. CR1 also includes ARPE bit 7.

Read CNT before/after and use uint16 subtraction across one wrap to measure µs in stats.

```c
RCC->APBENR2 |= RCC_APBENR2_TIM14EN;
TIM14->PSC = (uint16_t)(SystemCoreClock / 1000000u - 1u);
TIM14->ARR = 0xFFFFu;
TIM14->EGR = TIM_EGR_UG;
TIM14->CR1 = TIM_CR1_CEN;
```

| Register / function | Width, value and bit fields |
|---|---|
| RCC->APBENR2 | 32; 0, 11, 12, 14, 15 TIM14EN, 17, 18, 20 |
| TIM14->PSC  —  48 MHz / (47 + 1) = 1 MHz | 16 = 0x002F; 15:0 PSC |
| TIM14->ARR  —  full 16-bit range: wraps every 65.536 ms | 16 = 0xFFFF; 15:0 ARR |
| TIM14->CNT  —  read before and after each task, in µs | 16; 15:0 CNT |
| TIM14->EGR  —  UG: copy PSC into the counter now | 16 = 0x0001; 0 UG |
| TIM14->CR1 | 16 = 0x0001; 7 ARPE, 0 CEN |

Without EGR.UG, the initial roughly 65 ms interval uses 48 MHz rather than the divided microsecond timebase.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads levels; **MODER** selects mode; **AFR** selects alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal. Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly.

**Inertia** resists angular acceleration; **torque** turns the body. Opposite wheel forces spin the disc.

The disc inertia is I=mr²/2 with m=0.5 kg and r=55 mm. Half wheelbase b=45 mm.

sections.title: What Carries Forward
sourceHeadings: Slide 27: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
Shared contracts, isolated memory, synchronized sensing and measured time budgets make independent strategies comparable.

Fixed contracts, memory and time budgets let teams exchange brains without exchanging internals. Simulate physics while preserving real strategy C.

Reproducibility needs RNG isolation, same-instant sensing, no hidden state and consistent arithmetic. Final projects reuse this RTOS/display/world pattern and measured, replayable results.

sections.title: Board connections and controls
sourceHeadings: The Board: This Lesson's Pins
sections.body:
**ADC** converts voltage to numbers. **USART** uses **TX/RX** (transmit/receive); **I²C** uses **SDA/SCL** (data/clock). **OLED** is the display; **GND** is ground and **3V3** is 3.3 V. A **watchdog** checks software progress.

Nucleo-C031C6/MB1717 exposes outer ST morpho double rows and inner Arduino A0–A5/D0–D15 rows. Some signals share labels, for example PA5/D13.

Use the actual connected header position. Power is 3V3 and GND.

PA0/PA1 are joystick ADC IN0/IN1. PA4 is ADC IN4 for the knob.

PA2/PA3 USART2 TX/RX. PA6 TIM3_CH1 buzzer.

PB8/PB9 I²C1 SCL/SDA for OLED at 0x3C. PB4/PB5 buttons A/B and PB3 stick select.

Buttons, joystick and knob feed the application. PA5 blinks while watchdog refresh is permitted.

PA5 is the onboard LD4 output.

sections.title: GPIO port configuration
sourceHeadings: The Chip: The Same Pins, as Port Bits
sections.body:
**GPIO** means general-purpose input/output. **IDR** reads levels; **MODER** selects mode; **AFR** selects alternate function (**AF**). A **nibble** is four bits. **SWD** means Serial Wire Debug. **Pull-ups** hold open inputs high.

Each GPIO port has 16 pin bits. Pin n maps to IDR bit n, MODER bits 2n+1:2n and AFR nibble 4n (in the correct AFR bank).

MODER encodings are 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate, 11 analog. PA0/PA1/PA4 are analog.

PA2/PA3 and PA6 alternate AF1. PB8/PB9 alternate AF6.

PB3/PB4/PB5 inputs. PA13/PA14 remain SWD.

I²C pins need **open-drain** outputs (drive low, release high) and pull-ups.

PA5 is output for LD4. Board location and peripheral register bit are two views of the same MCU signal.

Select both mode and alternate-function number correctly. Buttons/select use pull-ups.

sourceHeadings: Slide 2: What a Good Embedded Project Looks Like
sections.body:
A **deadline** is the latest permitted completion time. **Fault injection** introduces a problem to check the response. Demonstrate behaviour against numeric limits.

A successful project finishes one clear behaviour, gives numeric limits, meets deadlines, handles faults predictably and can be explained by its authors. The table links each property to evidence: short demo, stats, overrun count, fault injection and oral.

A small complete measured game can score better than many unfinished features. Evidence supports engineering quality.

| **does one thing well** | one clear behaviour, finished | the 30-second demo |
| **has numbers** | every requirement has a unit and a limit | report table, `stats` |
| **meets its deadlines** | each task's worst response < its period | `stats` → `over` column = 0 |
| **survives faults** | a hung task, a missing device, a bad input: defined behaviour | fault demo with `hang` |

sourceHeadings: Slide 3: Four Tracks

**Software-in-the-loop (SITL)** runs controller C against modeled sensors. The **host** PC exercises portable logic before board integration.

Four tracks are game, drone, robot or an agreed original app-board idea. The table names starting lessons and engineering difficulties.

Drone/robot projects preserve SITL sensor/actuator boundaries. Game logic uses app_step(dt, pad) similarly.

sections.title: Track A — Games
sourceHeadings: Slide 4: Track A — Games
sections.body:
**Input-to-pixel latency** is action-to-visible-effect time. **Fuzzing** uses varied random inputs to expose boundary failures.

Game options include a complete arcade game with title/levels/high-score across rounds, substantial animation/particle/table-driven sound/replay extensions, or serial two-player/Python-opponent play. Console hardware is 128×64 OLED, stick, two buttons, knob and buzzer.

Required measurements are sustained frame rate, input-to-pixel latency, I²C bytes/frame and hours of random-input fuzz without screen escape or overflow.

sections.title: Track B — Drone
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: Track B — Drone
sections.body:
**Settling time** measures remaining near a target; **overshoot** measures travel beyond it. Measure fault detection and subsequent action separately.

Drone options are new mission planning such as survey/moving target/marker landing, a demonstrably improved cascaded or scheduled controller, or motor/IMU/link fault tolerance. MCU safety remains onboard while Python plans.

Required numbers are step settling/overshoot, worst mission attitude error and fault-to-detection-to-action time. Define land/hold/return responses rather than merely detecting a fault.

sections.title: Track C — Robot
sourceHeadings: Slide 6: Track C — Robot

**N** is trial count; a **seed** reproduces disturbances/starts. **Control-step cost** is CPU time for one decision.

Robot options include wall following/object pushing/map-free maze behaviour, a sumo strategy or a noisy synthesised new sensor. Start from line/navigation/balance/sumo lessons.

Report lap time or win rate over stated N seeded runs, worst tracking error and target CPU/control-step cost. One lucky run cannot demonstrate robustness.

A new sensor must appear in both world synthesis and controller use.

Track D needs an agreed measurable scope, base-board simulation and a pure-C core testable on the host.

An original idea must run on the base board in Wokwi, have a pure-C host-testable core and an instructor-approved numeric week 1 scope. Catalogue additions such as MPU 6050 at 0x68, buttons or LEDs are permitted while preserving the base board.

sections.title: Scope — MVP First
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: Scope — MVP First
sections.body:
A **subsystem** is one internal part. An **MVP** connects parts into a complete usable experience before stretch features.

Define MVP as no more than three end-to-end requirement lines for week 4. Target is the week 6 promise, stretch begins only after target is completed/tested/measured.

A playable ugly one-level app with timing and tests is an MVP. Physics without any usable display is only a subsystem.

Keeping each week demonstrable lets difficult weeks remove features without destroying the demo.

sourceHeadings: Slide 9: Requirements Are Numbers
sections.body:
Each **requirement** needs units, limit and measurement method. Add worst-case stage waits to estimate input response.

The table gives numeric examples for frames, latency, tracking, step response, fuzz/reset and idle/stacks.

Template input 10 ms+app 20 ms+display 50 ms already totals 80 ms worst case before I²C, so it cannot promise 70 ms input-to-pixel unchanged. Wish-like statements belong in stretch until a measurement exists.

sections.title: The Architecture Template
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: The Architecture Template
sections.body:
A **mailbox** transfers requests; a **snapshot** copies related fields; a **heartbeat** reports task progress. **IWDG** means independent watchdog.

Input 100 Hz/priority 5 owns pad and TIM3 sound. App 50 Hz/4 owns app state.

Telemetry 10 Hz/3 uses print_lock. Display 20 Hz/2 uses app_lock and bus_lock.

Health 4 Hz/1 checks heartbeats and refreshes 1 s IWDG. Shell exposes diagnostics.

Controls cross as sticky edges, sound as mailbox and state as protected snapshots. Redraw this architecture for the project with every arrow's protection labelled.

sections.title: Tasks, Rates, Priorities
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Tasks, Rates, Priorities
sections.body:
A **task** is scheduled work. **Polling** checks hardware while consuming CPU; a **blocked task** waits without doing so.

The task table defines input/app/telem/display/health/shell/idle periods and priorities. Display 50 ms is below telemetry 100 ms despite rate-monotonic ordering, because its polled 25 ms transfer may wait while telemetry timestamps should stay timely.

Health is low so runaway higher tasks prevent refresh. Shell blocks on UART and neither requires periodic heartbeat.

| Task | Period | Prio | Work | Beats? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `input` | 10 ms | 5 | `pad_read()`, sound mailbox, `beep_poll()` | yes |
| `app` | 20 ms | 4 | `app_step(20, &pad)` | yes |
| `telem` | 100 ms | 3 | `$APP` every run, `$SYS` every 10th | yes |
| `display` | 50 ms | 2 | `app_draw()`, `oled_flush()` | yes |
| `health` | 250 ms | 1 | `health_check()`, IWDG refresh, LD4 | — |
| `shell` | on input | 1 | blocks in `uart_getc()` | — |
| `idle` | — | 0 | the kernel's | — |

sections.title: Who Protects What
sourceHeadings: Slide 13: Who Protects What
sections.body:
A **critical section** briefly prevents interruption; a **mutex** protects work by one task at a time. **Priority inheritance** boosts a blocking lock owner.

The table gives protection rules. Copy the 10 B pad briefly; publish the sound flag last. Use mutexes for longer work and print_lock for whole lines.

Each heartbeat/timing counter has one owner. Clearing is a request.

Priority inheritance boosts display to app priority 4 when it holds app_lock that app needs.

| Shared thing | Writers → readers | Tool | Why that tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| controls (`pad_t`) | input → app | critical section | 10-byte copy, a few cycles |
| sound request | app → input | one-slot mailbox, flag written last | input is TIM3's only owner |
| app state | app → display, telem | `app_lock` mutex | drawing takes long enough to be preempted |
| I²C1 | display, shell (`scan`) | `bus_lock` mutex | a transfer is ~0.1–25 ms |
| the UART | everyone | `print_lock`, whole lines | lesson 08 |
| heartbeats | each task → health | **one counter per task** | single writer: no lock at all |
| `prof[]` timing | each task → shell | single writer + clear *request* | the shell never writes a counter |

Priority inheritance is enabled by OS_PRIORITY_INHERIT=1.
